Threat: Braking & Safety ECU Command Suppression / Safety System Disablement
Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: An attacker with access to the vehicle’s internal networks (through compromised infotainment, telematics, OBD-II, or a breached gateway ECU) can inject spoofed or high-priority CAN frames that override or suppress legitimate braking, ABS, ESC, or airbag control messages. Because many braking and safety ECUs rely on unauthenticated, real-time CAN traffic, the attacker can block critical sensor inputs, disable actuator commands, or send false states that trick the system into thinking conditions are normal. This can result in brakes failing to engage, airbags failing to deploy during a crash, or safety interventions (ABS/ESC) being silently disabled. The outcome is direct compromise of occupant safety with high risk of injury or fatality.
Attacker goal / impact: Prevent brakes or airbags from deploying during an emergency.
Mitigation: Hardware-Enforced Safety Overrides and Fail-Safe Operating Modes
Mitigation definition: Implement hardware-level safety systems (independent brake actuators, backup crash sensors, and non-bypassable airbag initiation circuits) that continue functioning even if the CAN bus is compromised, ensuring braking and airbag activation cannot be disabled via network commands.

Mitigation: Secure Gateway Filtering With Safety-Critical Message Authentication
Mitigation definition: Route all braking and safety-related CAN traffic through a hardened secure gateway that enforces message authentication, ID whitelisting, and rate limits, blocking spoofed or manipulated frames from suppressing brake commands or disabling airbag deployment logic.

Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: A malicious device attached to the CAN network can masquerade as a legitimate ECU. It can send control commands or respond to queries to mislead other modules. Without message authentication, the vehicle cannot differentiate between genuine and fake ECUs.
Attacker goal / impact: A compromised non-critical ECU (e.g., Radio) pretends to be the Safety ECU to send fake commands.
Mitigation: ECU Identity Verification With Message Authentication and Secure Gateways
Mitigation definition: Require all CAN traffic to pass through a secure gateway that enforces message authentication (MACs, digital signatures, or link-layer authentication where supported) and validates sender identity against an authorized ECU list, ensuring forged or spoofed devices cannot masquerade as legitimate modules.

Mitigation definition: Isolate critical ECUs on protected CAN segments and enforce strict ID filtering and ECU whitelisting so only approved modules can transmit on specific message IDs or bus zones, preventing malicious devices from injecting spoofed control frames or responding on behalf of trusted ECUs.

Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: Modern vehicles use central gateways to isolate CAN subnets (powertrain, chassis, body). A compromised gateway ECU can bridge malicious messages across domains. This allows attackers to escalate from infotainment or telematics systems into safety-critical networks.
Attacker goal / impact: The "Holy Grail" attack: Breaking the segmentation between Infotainment and CAN Bus.
Mitigation: Hardened Gateway ECUs With Domain Isolation and Message Authentication
Mitigation definition: Implement strict domain isolation within the central gateway and enforce message authentication, ID filtering, and policy-based routing so even if a non-critical domain is compromised, malicious traffic cannot be bridged or forwarded into safety-critical CAN segments.

Mitigation definition: Protect the gateway ECU with signed firmware, locked-down diagnostic/update interfaces, and runtime monitoring of cross-domain traffic patterns, immediately blocking or alerting on anomalous bridging behaviors that could indicate compromise or lateral movement from infotainment or telematics systems.

Threat: Lateral movement to CAN or vehicle control networks
Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: If the infotainment system shares a bridge or gateway with the vehicle’s CAN bus, a compromise may spread to safety-critical ECUs. This allows attackers to manipulate braking, steering, or sensor systems indirectly. Network segmentation flaws greatly amplify this risk.
Attacker goal / impact: Moving from a compromised Wifi/Bluetooth entry point into the safety network.
Mitigation: Secure Gateway Enforcement With Anomaly Detection and Access Controls
Mitigation definition: Use a hardened central gateway that authenticates cross-domain traffic, blocks unauthorized service requests, and monitors for abnormal message patterns or attempted domain escalation, preventing compromised infotainment components from sending or relaying commands to vehicle-control networks.

Threat: Lateral movement to CAN or vehicle control networks
Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)

Mitigation: Strong Network Segmentation With Isolated Safety-Critical Domains
Mitigation definition: Physically and logically isolate infotainment, telematics, and connectivity modules from safety-critical CAN networks, enforcing strict gateway policies, message filtering, and one-way dataflows so that a compromise in an internet-facing subsystem cannot propagate into braking, steering, or powertrain ECUs.

Threat: ADAS Sensor Manipulation / Assistance System Degradation
Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: An attacker who compromises vehicle networks or ADAS sensor inputs (camera, radar, ultrasonic, or LiDAR) can disrupt or falsify data fed into the Advanced Driver Assistance ECU. By injecting spoofed CAN messages, jamming or blinding sensors, or suppressing perception data, the attacker can cause lane-keeping systems to drift, adaptive cruise control to misjudge distance, or parking assistance to fail. Since ADAS depends on real-time, accurate sensor fusion, these manipulations can disable lane guidance, create unsafe following behavior, or cause the ECU to ignore obstacles. In extreme cases, the system may apply incorrect steering, braking, or acceleration, putting occupants and bystanders at risk.
Components affected: Lane keeping, adaptive cruise control, and parking sensors
Attacker goal / impact: Cause the vehicle to ignore obstacles or brake unnecessarily (phantom braking).
Mitigation: Fail-Safe ADAS Modes With Redundant Perception Paths
Mitigation definition: Provide redundant sensing (camera + radar + ultrasonic), enforce safe fallback behavior when perception degrades (e.g., disengage ACC, limit steering assistance), and isolate ADAS ECUs from untrusted network domains, ensuring assistance systems fail safely instead of applying unsafe control actions.

Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: Attackers can flood the CAN bus with high-priority frames, monopolizing bandwidth and preventing legitimate traffic. This can disable safety-critical systems or cause unpredictable ECU behavior. The system may appear frozen or enter a fail-safe mode.
Attacker goal / impact: Flood the CAN bus to freeze ECU communications; vehicle enters "limp mode" or shuts down.
Mitigation: Rate-Limiting and Priority Enforcement at Secure Gateways
Mitigation definition: Use a secure gateway ECU to enforce per-ID rate limits, validate arbitration priority usage, and drop frames that exceed allowable transmission frequency so attackers cannot monopolize CAN bandwidth or suppress legitimate safety-critical traffic.

Mitigation: Segmented CAN Networks With DoS-Resilient Isolation
Mitigation definition: Isolate safety-critical ECUs on protected CAN segments and use bus guardians or hardware firewalls to block excessive or malformed traffic from non-critical domains, ensuring essential control and sensor messages continue to flow even during a flooding attempt.

Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: Standardized diagnostic protocols like UDS (Unified Diagnostic Services) allow access to memory, fault codes, and even firmware updates. If not properly restricted, attackers can use these interfaces to alter configurations or reprogram ECUs. Remote attacks are possible when the diagnostic stack is exposed via telematics or infotainment gateways.
Attacker goal / impact: Bypass authentication to inject CAN messages via physical port (Key cloning, theft).
Mitigation: Access-Controlled Diagnostic Modes With Strong Authentication
Mitigation definition: Restrict advanced UDS services (programming, memory access, configuration changes) to authenticated dealer tools or authorized service equipment, using secure challenge–response protocols and PINs/keys so attackers cannot invoke privileged diagnostic functions through OBD-II or remote gateways.

Mitigation definition: Route all diagnostic requests through a secure, policy-enforcing gateway ECU that filters UDS/OBD-II commands, blocks high-risk services by default, and isolates telematics or infotainment domains from the internal vehicle networks, preventing remote or unauthorized diagnostic access from reaching critical ECUs.

Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: If attackers gain access to diagnostic ports or OTA update systems, they can overwrite ECU firmware. This may install persistent malware or modify control logic. Unsigned or poorly verified firmware updates make this attack feasible.
Attacker goal / impact: Permanently alter vehicle behavior, remove speed limiters, or disable safety features.
Mitigation: Cryptographically Signed Firmware and Secure Boot Enforcement
Mitigation definition: Require all ECU firmware and OTA packages to be cryptographically signed by a trusted OEM key, verify signatures and version metadata before any update is applied, and enforce secure boot so only verified firmware images can execute, blocking unauthorized or tampered reflashes.

Mitigation: Hardened Update and Diagnostic Access Controls
Mitigation definition: Restrict access to diagnostic ports and OTA update interfaces with strong authentication, role-based permissions, and locked-down reprogramming modes, and log all reflashing events, preventing untrusted tools or actors from initiating firmware updates outside approved service and OEM processes.

Threat: Engine & Powertrain ECU Overload / Destructive DoS
Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: An attacker who gains access to the powertrain CAN domain (via compromised gateway, telematics, OBD-II, or lateral movement) can flood the Engine Control Unit (ECU) with high-frequency or malformed control messages. By overwhelming the ECU’s processing capacity or suppressing critical sensor data (e.g., temperature, RPM, oil pressure), the attacker can induce incorrect engine behavior. This may disable safety limiters or cause the ECU to miss protective shutdown thresholds, allowing the engine to over-rev, overheat, or run without proper fuel/air balance, leading to catastrophic mechanical failure (“engine blowout”) or permanent damage.
Attacker goal / impact: Cause physical damage to the engine (overheating, over-revving) via repeated commands.
Mitigation: Engine Safety Limiters Enforced at Hardware and ECU Levels
Mitigation definition: Implement hardware-level rev-limiters, temperature cutoffs, and fail-safe operating modes that cannot be overridden by CAN messages, ensuring protective shutdown systems remain functional even if the ECU is saturated or receiving malicious inputs.

Threat: Engine & Powertrain ECU Overload / Destructive DoS
Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)

Mitigation definition: Enforce message authentication, CAN ID whitelisting, and strict rate limits at the central secure gateway to prevent attackers from flooding the Engine ECU with spoofed or excessive control commands, ensuring the ECU cannot be overwhelmed into unsafe operating states.

Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: If ECUs do not enforce secure boot, attackers can load modified or malicious firmware images. This can persist even after power cycles and evade standard diagnostics. Secure boot validation failure is a major vector for long-term compromise.
Attacker goal / impact: Bypass trust chain to load malicious OS or firmware on ECUs.
Mitigation: Locked-Down Bootloader Access and Controlled Update Paths
Mitigation definition: Disable or restrict bootloader reprogramming interfaces, require authenticated flashing sessions through approved service tools, and log or alert on any bootloader access attempts, ensuring attackers cannot exploit open or poorly protected boot modes to install persistent malicious firmware.

Mitigation definition: Enforce secure boot on all ECUs by establishing a hardware-backed root of trust that validates firmware signatures, version metadata, and integrity before execution, preventing any unsigned or tampered boot images from loading—even after reboots or power cycles.

Threat: Memory corruption or buffer overflow in ECU software
Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: Bugs in ECU firmware parsers or network stacks can lead to memory corruption when malformed CAN or diagnostic packets are received. Attackers can exploit these vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code. This is especially dangerous when firmware runs with high privilege.
Attacker goal / impact: Crash an ECU or execute arbitrary code via malformed packets.
Mitigation: Input Validation and Gateway-Level Sanitization of Network Traffic
Mitigation definition: Validate all inbound CAN, UDS, and diagnostic payloads at a secure gateway ECU, enforcing protocol correctness, length limits, and service-level restrictions so malformed or oversized packets never reach vulnerable modules, reducing exploitation opportunities against high-privilege ECU firmware.

Threat: Memory corruption or buffer overflow in ECU software
Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: Bugs in ECU firmware parsers or network stacks can lead to memory corruption when malformed CAN or diagnostic packets are received. Attackers can exploit these vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code. This is especially dangerous when firmware runs with high privilege.
Attacker goal / impact: Crash an ECU or execute arbitrary code via malformed packets.
Mitigation: Memory-Safe Parsing, Bounds Enforcement, and Hardened Firmware Builds
Mitigation definition: Use strict bounds checking, validated parsing routines, and safe memory-handling patterns in ECU firmware, combined with compiler hardening features (stack canaries, ASLR, DEP, and fortified libc) to prevent malformed CAN or diagnostic packets from triggering memory corruption or enabling arbitrary code execution.

Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: Captured legitimate messages can be replayed at a later time to trigger vehicle actions without authorization. For example, replaying a door-unlock or engine-start command. CAN’s stateless design makes it difficult to distinguish old messages from current ones.
Attacker goal / impact: Capture and re-send valid commands (e.g., "Unlock Door") to trigger actions without auth.
Mitigation: Message Freshness Enforcement With Counters, Nonces, or Timestamps
Mitigation definition: Introduce freshness checks at the secure gateway or ECU level—such as rolling counters, monotonic timestamps, or nonce-based challenges—so each CAN message is validated as “new” and any replayed or out-of-sequence frames are rejected before reaching critical modules.

Mitigation definition: Route CAN traffic through a secure gateway that enforces contextual validation (expected timing, message frequency, and ECU state), blocking messages that repeat too quickly or appear outside their normal operational window, preventing attackers from replaying captured commands like unlock or start signals.

Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: Attackers can inject forged messages onto the CAN bus to impersonate legitimate ECUs. Since the CAN protocol lacks authentication, other modules may accept and act on malicious commands. This can directly manipulate vehicle behavior, such as disabling brakes or spoofing sensor data.
Attacker goal / impact: Send fabricated messages to control steering, acceleration, or braking.
Mitigation: Secure Gateways With Message Authentication and Signal Validation
Mitigation definition: Route all CAN traffic through a secure gateway ECU that enforces message-level authentication, verifies signal plausibility, and blocks packets from untrusted sources, ensuring forged or out-of-context CAN frames cannot reach safety-critical modules or control surfaces.

Mitigation definition: Isolate safety-critical ECUs on protected CAN segments and restrict write permissions to authorized modules only, using firewalling, ID filtering, and rate-limiting at the network layer to prevent unauthorized devices from injecting commands or flooding bus traffic.

Threat: Key or credential leakage from ECUs
Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)
Description: Some ECUs store cryptographic keys or authentication tokens insecurely in flash or RAM. Physical attackers can extract these through chip-off or debugging interfaces. Once leaked, these secrets allow reprogramming, cloning, or remote unlocking of other vehicles.
Attacker goal / impact: Extract cryptographic keys to decrypt firmware or spoof valid messages.
Mitigation: Hardware-Backed Secure Key Storage and Non-Extractable Secrets
Mitigation definition: Store all cryptographic keys, authentication tokens, and ECU credentials in hardware-backed secure elements or TPM-like modules, ensuring secrets are non-exportable, encrypted at rest, and never exposed directly in flash or RAM where chip-off or debug extraction attacks are possible.

Threat: Key or credential leakage from ECUs
Theme: Vehicle Control & Safety Critical (CAN Bus & ECUs)

Mitigation: Locked-Down Debug/Programming Interfaces With Secure Access Controls
Mitigation definition: Disable or tightly restrict JTAG, SWD, and other debug/programming interfaces on production ECUs, require authenticated and authorized service sessions for any access, and log all attempts, preventing attackers from extracting keys or internal secrets through physical probing or low-level diagnostic channels.

Description: Weak Bluetooth implementations or pairing protocols can allow attackers to eavesdrop, inject commands, or access internal data. Exploiting Bluetooth vulnerabilities may not require physical access if the vehicle’s pairing mode is active. Attackers can impersonate trusted devices or trigger DoS conditions.
Attacker goal / impact: Remote code execution or pairing without consent to access contacts or unlock the car.
Mitigation: Hardened Bluetooth Pairing and Authenticated Sessions
Mitigation definition: Enforce secure pairing modes (Just Works disabled where possible, prefer passkey/Numeric Comparison), require user interaction for new pairings, and bind Bluetooth sessions to authenticated, trusted device identities to prevent impersonation, unauthorized pairing, and eavesdropping on in-vehicle communications.

Mitigation: Restricted Bluetooth Attack Surface and Anomaly-Aware Handling
Mitigation definition: Limit Bluetooth-exposed services and commands to the minimum required, validate all inbound messages for format and authorization, and implement rate limiting and timeout handling so malformed packets, repeated pairing attempts, or unexpected commands cannot access internal data paths or trigger denial-of-service conditions.

Threat: Compromised mobile app integrations (Android Auto / CarPlay)
Description: When smartphones connect via Android Auto or Apple CarPlay, vulnerabilities in mobile apps or USB drivers can serve as attack vectors. Malware on the phone could exploit weak isolation between the mobile and infotainment environments. This creates a path for lateral movement into vehicle networks.
Attacker goal / impact: Use a compromised phone to send malicious input to the head unit.
Mitigation: Controlled USB / Wireless Interfaces With Policy Enforcement and Threat Detection
Mitigation definition: Restrict Android Auto / CarPlay interfaces to approved protocols and validated message types, apply strict filtering at the USB/wireless ingress point, and monitor for anomalous behavior from connected devices to prevent malware or tampered apps from abusing integration channels to reach in-vehicle networks.

Threat: Compromised mobile app integrations (Android Auto / CarPlay)

Malware on the phone could exploit weak isolation between the mobile and infotainment environments. This creates a path for lateral movement into vehicle networks.
Attacker goal / impact: Use a compromised phone to send malicious input to the head unit.
Mitigation: Strict Isolation and Sandboxing Between Mobile and Infotainment Domains
Mitigation definition: Enforce hardened isolation between Android Auto / CarPlay processes and the infotainment system, using sandboxing, containerization, and restricted IPC so connected mobile apps cannot access privileged interfaces or pivot into vehicle-side services, even if the phone is compromised.

Description: An attacker could exploit security misconfigurations to gain unauthorized access or functionality. This could include unpatched flaws, unprotected files, and directories, or default accounts.
Attacker goal / impact: Default passwords or open debug ports left on the Infotainment OS.
Mitigation: Harden Assets Against Attacks
Mitigation definition: Apply security best practices to reduce vulnerabilities in systems, applications, and infrastructure. This includes disabling unused services, enforcing strong configurations, patching known issues, and limiting exposed interfaces to minimize the attack surface.
How to implement: Identify and Prioritize critical assets - Disable unnecessary ports, services, and default accounts - Apply secure configuration baselines (e.g., CIS Benchmarks) -regularly patch systems and software - Use configuration Management tools for consistency - Monitor for configuration drift and misconfigurations - document and standardize hardening procedures for repeatability
Why it works: Hardening reduces the likelihood of compromise by minimizing exposure points attackers could exploit. This involves securing default configurations, limiting access, and maintaining consistent baselines across environments. It supports defense-in-depth by strengthening each component before it's exposed to internal or external threats.
Examples: Use AWS systems Manager or Azure Policy for config enforcement - Apply CIS Benchmarks for Windows, Linux, or cloud services - Use Ansible, Chef, or Puppet for consistent hardening - Disable unused services in EC2, GCE, or VMware instances - Apply Security Groups/firewall rules in AWS, Azure, or GCP - Use Amazon Inspector or Azure Defender for vulnerability Scans - patch using WSUS, SCCM, or Linux Package managers

Description: An attacker could exploit security misconfigurations to gain unauthorized access or functionality. This could include unpatched flaws, unprotected files, and directories, or default accounts.
Attacker goal / impact: Default passwords or open debug ports left on the Infotainment OS.
Mitigation: Implement a minimal installation
Mitigation definition: Use a minimal installation approach by configuring only essential features and frameworks. Regularly review and remove any unused components, files, and directories.
How to implement: Identify and install Only essential packages, services, and dependencies. - Remove default applications, modules, and libraries not required for operation. - Validate that updates don’t reintroduce unused or insecure features.
Why it works: Minimal installation starts with a secure baseline configuration containing only essential components, reducing the attack surface. Automated compliance checks and regular audits help detect misconfigurations.
Examples: Ansible can automate minimal package installs using roles and playbooks. Terraform defines infrastructure with only required resources, avoiding defaults.

Description: An attacker could exploit security misconfigurations to gain unauthorized access or functionality. This could include unpatched flaws, unprotected files, and directories, or default accounts.

Mitigation: Implement Timely Patching
Mitigation definition: Establish a robust patch management process to ensure timely updates for critical security components. Regularly monitor for vulnerabilities and apply patches immediately upon release. Prioritize patching based on severity and impact to maintain the integrity of your architecture.
How to implement: automate patch deployment to reduce errors and improve speed. - Have a rollback plan for failed patches. - Train staff on secure patching practices.
Why it works: Automated patch deployment reduces delays and minimizes human error, ensuring faster remediation of vulnerabilities. A rollback plan is essential to restore system stability in case a patch introduces issues. Training staff on secure patching practices increases awareness and ensures that updates are applied effectively without compromising system integrity or availability.
Examples: WSUS (Windows server update services): Automates patch distribution across Windows environments. - Ansible: Enables automated deployment and rollback of patches across servers. - JFrog Artifactory: Tracks and manages third-party Package versions for updates. - Azure update Manager / AWS systems Manager patch Manager: Automates patching in cloud infrastructure. - Qualys patch Management: Provides automation, rollback options, and patch compliance tracking.

Description: Attackers exploit vulnerabilities by injecting malicious code (e.g., JavaScript, SQL queries) into the mobile app.
Attacker goal / impact: Execute malicious scripts in the Infotainment browser/UI.
Mitigation: Implement Parameterization
Mitigation definition: Use parameterized queries and prepared statements to enforce strict separation of code and data in database and OS operations, preventing injection attacks. Ensure input values are bound to placeholders rather than concatenated into code strings.
How to implement: Enforce Use of parameterized APIs or libraries for all command and database operations. - Audit codebases to Identify and eliminate unsafe string concatenation. - Validate all input values before binding them to parameters. - ensure consistent Use of prepared statements in both backend and frontend frameworks. - regularly test parameter handling through code reviews and Security audits.
Why it works: Parameterization works by clearly separating user input from the command or query structure. Instead of injecting input directly into commands, parameters are used as placeholders, which prevents injection attacks. This technique ensures inputs are interpreted strictly as data, not executable code. Regular audits and validations help maintain its effectiveness, especially in preventing OS and database-level injection threats.
Examples: - For OS Command Injection, libraries like Apache Commons Exec and Python's subprocess module provide methods to safely execute commands with parameters. - In Python, use the subprocess.run(["cmd", param]) pattern. - In Java, use PreparedStatement to bind variables in SQL queries. - In web apps, frameworks like React escape inputs in templates, and libraries like DOMPurify sanitize HTML. - Use ORMs like SQLAlchemy or Entity Framework to enforce parameterization automatically.

Description: Attackers exploit vulnerabilities by injecting malicious code (e.g., JavaScript, SQL queries) into the mobile app.
Attacker goal / impact: Execute malicious scripts in the Infotainment browser/UI.
Mitigation: Validate User Input
Mitigation definition: Implement strict input validation to ensure user-provided data adheres to expected formats, types, and constraints. Reject or sanitize any input that does not meet these criteria to prevent potential security vulnerabilities such as injection attacks or unauthorized access.
How to implement: Use whitelisting for acceptable input formats and values. - implement regular expressions to Enforce input patterns. - limit input length to mitigate buffer overflow risks. - Validate data types explicitly - Employ context-aware encoding for output. -Add rate limiting to block brute-force input - Use Security libraries or frameworks with built-in validation. - Log and Monitor invalid input for analysis.
Why it works: Input validation ensures user data is clean, expected, and secure before processing. Strong validation prevents injection, overflow, and brute-force attacks. Input rules should align with business logic, and validation must happen both client- and server-side. Monitoring rejected inputs can help identify attack patterns and improve defenses over time.
Examples: - Joi (Node.js): Define and enforce input schemas using clear syntax - Validator.js: Validate and sanitize strings (e.g., emails, URLs) - Express-validator: Middleware for input validation in Express apps - Yup (JavaScript/TypeScript): Schema validation for form inputs - OWASP ESAPI: Java library for input validation and encoding

Description: A malicious USB stick or device can deliver payloads when connected to the media or diagnostic port. These can exploit parsing vulnerabilities in file systems or firmware loaders. Such attacks are particularly dangerous because they often bypass network-based defenses.
Attacker goal / impact: Fuzzing the USB stack to crash the Infotainment OS or gain shell access.
Mitigation: Restricted USB Functionality With Strict Parsing and Allowed Device Profiles
Mitigation definition: Limit USB interfaces to approved device classes (media-only, charging-only, no HID/emulation) and enforce hardened parsing for file systems and media formats, ensuring malformed or crafted USB content cannot trigger parser vulnerabilities or arbitrary code execution in infotainment or diagnostic components.

Description: A malicious USB stick or device can deliver payloads when connected to the media or diagnostic port. These can exploit parsing vulnerabilities in file systems or firmware loaders. Such attacks are particularly dangerous because they often bypass network-based defenses.

Mitigation definition: Require user approval or service-mode authentication before enabling privileged USB operations (e.g., firmware loading or diagnostic access), and block automatic execution of scripts or update files, preventing malicious USB devices from bypassing network defenses to deliver payloads or manipulate ECU systems.

Description: Voice-recognition interfaces can be tricked by ultrasonic or hidden audio commands (so-called “silent speech attacks”). Attacker goal / impact: Using hidden audio frequencies or recorded voice to trigger commands (e.g., "Open Garage").

Mitigation definition: Minimize voice data sent to third-party servers by preferring on-device processing where possible, encrypt all transmitted audio, and restrict the assistant’s access to contacts, messages, and vehicle/system controls to least-privilege scopes, reducing both command-abuse impact and privacy leakage if voice traffic is intercepted or misused.

Logs are structured to separate sensitive data from general information, utilizing data masking techniques. Logs are encrypted during transmission and storage. Automated tools analyze logs for anomalies, and alerts are generated for suspicious activities. Log access is restricted to authorized personnel only, with regular audits to ensure compliance and effectiveness.
Examples: Splunk: Log analysis and alerting - ELK Stack: logging and visualization - Graylog: Real-time Log Management - HashiCorp Vault: secure Log storage - IBM QRadar and Microsoft Sentinel: SIEM solutions with anomaly detection

Description: An attacker could exploit broken access control to access unauthorized functionality and data, such as accessing other users' accounts, viewing sensitive files, modifying other users’ data, and changing access rights.
Attacker goal / impact: User A accessing User B's vehicle telemetry or location data.
Mitigation: Deny Access by Default
Mitigation definition: Enforce a deny-by-default access control policy, where no user, system, or plugin is granted access unless explicitly allowed by defined rules. Default behavior should reject all requests until specific permissions are granted through access policies or allow-lists.
How to implement: Define explicit allow-lists for all actions, users, services, and data access. - Configure default access controls to deny any request unless explicitly authorized. - ensure all new plugins, APIs, and user roles are evaluated for access restrictions before deployment. - Review access control configurations regularly to ensure no implicit permissions exist. - Enforce access policies through infrastructure-as-code or configuration Management to prevent misconfigurations.
Why it works: Deny-by-default policies ensure that access is never assumed or open by default. Instead, each access request must meet pre-approved conditions before being granted. This limits the potential attack surface and prevents unauthorized interactions. By configuring allow-lists and enforcing explicit permissions at every layer—from API gateways to internal services, organizations prevent unintended access. Regular audits help detect and remove outdated or overly permissive rules.
Examples: - AWS IAM: IAM policies can be configured to deny all access unless specifically allowed via policies. - Google Cloud IAM uses allow-based roles where no access is granted until explicitly permitted. - API Gateways: Only routes explicitly defined in the gateway are reachable; others are denied by default. - Azure Resource Manager enforces deny-by-default behavior in RBAC assignments. - Kubernetes Network Policies deny all pod-to-pod communication by default unless allow-rules are defined.

Description: Excessively collecting, storing, processing, or sharing personal data. The data minimization principle is critical here: only the strictly necessary data should be collected or disclosed. Data disclosure can be explicit, i.e., intended or designed by the system, or implicit, i.e., unintended or indirect (e.g., through metadata or derived from other data). The focus is on four threat characteristics: Unnecessary data types: this relates to the data type sensitivity, granularity, and encoding, which can be too detailed Excessive data volume: this relates to the amount and frequency of the data processing and the number of involved data subjects, which can be too high Unnecessary processing: this relates to the further data treatment analysis, propagation, or retention, which can be considered not strictly necessary Excessive exposure: this relates to the different parties with whom the data is shared, which can be considered too much, and how widely accessible the data is

Mitigation: Implement Access Control Measures
Mitigation definition: Implement robust access control mechanisms to validate and authorize each entity's actions within the system. Ensure that permissions are strictly enforced to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive data and functionality. Regularly review and update access controls to address vulnerabilities and adhere to the principle of least privilege.
How to implement: Define clear access policies based on job responsibilities and data sensitivity - Use least privilege as a default for all roles and permissions - Separate duties across roles to reduce risk from over-privileged accounts - Review and update access rights regularly, especially after role changes - Apply fine-grained access control at the resource, function, and data level
Why it works: Access control ensures users and systems only access what they need based on roles and responsibilities. By applying least privilege and separating duties, organizations reduce the risk of abuse or error. Fine-grained controls restrict access to specific data or functions, and regular reviews ensure permissions stay aligned with evolving roles.
Examples: AWS IAM / Azure RBAC: Define and manage granular role-based access - Okta / Keycloak: Centralize user role Management and access policies - OPA (Open Policy Agent): Enforce fine-grained access at the application level - GitLab / GitHub roles: control project and repository access by role - GCP IAM Conditions: Apply attribute-based access rules for resources

Mitigation: Implement Code Obfuscation
Mitigation definition: Use code obfuscation techniques to make your mobile app's source and machine code difficult to interpret.
How to implement: Choose robust Obfuscation tools that are regularly updated to counter new reverse engineering techniques. - combine Obfuscation with other Security measures, such as encryption and secure coding practices, for layered protection. - regularly evaluate the effectiveness of Obfuscation methods against current reverse engineering tools. - Educate developers on the importance of secure coding and Obfuscation practices.
Why it works: Code obfuscation transforms readable source code into a harder-to-understand version without changing its behavior. This makes reverse engineering more difficult. It typically includes renaming identifiers, altering control flow, and inserting dummy code. Automated build tools help integrate obfuscation into development pipelines, and regular updates ensure resistance to evolving analysis methods.
Examples: - ProGuard: A tool for Android that shrinks, optimizes, and obfuscates code. - DexGuard: An advanced version of ProGuard with extra Android security. - R8: A modern code shrinker and obfuscator for Android apps. - ConfuserEx: An open-source .NET obfuscator. - JavaGuard: A Java obfuscator to prevent reverse engineering. - DashO: A commercial tool for Java and Android with advanced obfuscation.
